lesson.title: Lists Change, Strings Don't: Understanding Mutability
lesson.summary: Lists can be modified in place after they are created, unlike immutable strings, and that difference has real consequences for variables that share a list.
lesson.body:
You learned that strings are immutable: once a string is created, you cannot change one of its characters in place. Something like name[0] = "J" raises a TypeError, and the only way to "change" a string is to build an entirely new one and reassign the variable to it. Lists break that rule completely. A list is mutable, meaning you can change, add, or remove its contents after it is created, without ever creating a new list object.

The simplest form of mutation is item assignment: use indexing on the left side of an equals sign to overwrite a single element in place.

original = [1, 2, 3]
alias = original
alias[0] = 99
print(original)
print(alias is original)

This example is where mutability gets genuinely important to understand, not just as a feature but as a source of bugs. The line alias = original does not copy the list; it makes alias point to the exact same list object that original already points to, the same way two nicknames can refer to the same person. When alias[0] = 99 modifies that shared object, the change is visible through both names, because there was only ever one list. print(original) shows [99, 2, 3], not [1, 2, 3], even though the code never mentioned original by name when making the change. print(alias is original) confirms this with True, since is checks whether two variables refer to the identical object in memory, not just equal-looking contents.

This is a sharp contrast with strings and numbers. If original had been a string and you wrote alias = original, then later changed alias by rebuilding it with alias = alias + "!", original would be completely untouched, because that operation creates a new string object and points alias at it, leaving the original object, and original's reference to it, exactly as it was. Lists do not get that automatic protection, because in-place mutation changes the one shared object that every variable pointing to it can see.

When you genuinely want an independent copy rather than a second name for the same list, slicing gives you a clean way to get one, since you already know from the previous concept that a slice always builds a new list.

copy_list = original[:]
copy_list[0] = -1
print(original)
print(copy_list)

original[:] slices the entire list from start to end, which produces a new list object with the same current contents, [99, 2, 3]. Modifying copy_list[0] to -1 only affects that new object, so print(original) still shows [99, 2, 3], unchanged, while print(copy_list) shows [-1, 2, 3]. The rule to carry forward is simple: assignment (=) shares a reference to a list, it never copies it, while slicing, and the list methods you are about to learn, give you explicit, deliberate ways to either mutate the original or build something separate. Knowing which one you are doing at every step is the single most important habit for avoiding list-related bugs.
